name: Taiof
catalog_citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Taiof. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages (Curzon Language Family Series), 426-439. Richmond: Curzon. (archive.org scan of the 2011 Routledge reprint)
catalog_locator: p. 427, §1.2 'Phonotactics and stress' (PDF p. 444 of, running head 'TAIOF 427')
catalog_quote: Stress tends to be word-initial in citation forms, but to shift in continuous speech. All syllables are pronounced relatively fully. These observations suggest that Taiof is a syllable-counting language rather than one with metrical stress, but this requires further research.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In isolation (citation forms) stress falls on the first syllable of the word; in connected speech its position shifts, and there is no vowel reduction, so the author doubts that Taiof has genuine metrical word stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the author hedges the whole statement ('tends to', 'requires further research') and notes stress shifts in continuous speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly about citation forms of words; position in continuous speech said to shift (phrase-level effects not described). Description based on material from two Taiof speakers (Josephine Tosan, Rose Sisip); applies to the Taiof dialect, not necessarily to mainland Saposa.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Ross's sketch of TAIOF (Glottolog dialect taio1240 under sapo1253 Saposa; WALS code taf), spoken on Taiof Island; Ross notes Saposa (mainland villages, = Nuclear Saposa nucl1495) is Taiof's closest relative but different enough 'to warrant separate descriptions'. The only description of Saposa proper, Kennedy & Kennedy 1977 'Saposa phonemes', is not available online.
